chapter_theme: Under the heading கீழ்மக்கள் இயல்பு, seventeen verses argue that the base cannot be changed: good company, instruction, a ruler's grant, punishment, favour and wealth all leave them as they were, and the wise neither trust them, counsel them nor honour them in place of the great. Three verses (96, 103, 106) tie baseness to a way of life, a line of descent or family rank.

90.reading: The roaring sea does not lose its salt though great floods of fresh water pour into it, and in the same way the base never come to goodness of mind, however good the company they keep.
90.nuance: Lines 3-4 turn the wording of a familiar couplet inside out: இனநலம் நன்குடைய ராயினும் ... மனநலம் ஆகா, good company in full, and still no good mind. The image is chosen against the idea that water takes on the nature of what it meets: the sea takes in the river and stays salt.

pazhamozhi.literal: the base never become good of mind

story.act: no story; the proverb states the nature of the base as a type, matched by the salt sea

pazhamozhi.applied_to: good company cannot reform the base

91.reading: Those who have joined the worthy and live as their own people do not go over to the small, even when the small are said to be superior, for, as the verse asks the lord of the fertile town of cranes, can anyone eat sand that has jaggery mixed into it?
91.nuance: The proverb grants the small some sweetness (அக்காரம்) and still calls them sand: a little attraction does not make the mixture fit to take in. மிக்காரால் என்று is compressed; it may mean 'thinking them great' or 'because others say they are great'.

pazhamozhi.literal: can sand mixed with jaggery be eaten?

story.act: no story; the proverb is an image of something sweetened but still inedible

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those settled among the worthy do not take up with the small, whatever is said for them

92.reading: The verse asks whether the angry men of cruel work can do what those whose character is to do their own proper work do, and answers with the proverb that not everything ploughed counts as a harvest.
92.nuance: நந்துழுத can be divided நம் உழுத, 'what we ploughed', or நந்து உழுத, 'what the snail ploughed'; on the second, the snail's trail looks like a furrow and is not one, which suits the contrast between the base and the worthy better. Either way the claim is that the look of work is not its yield.

pazhamozhi.literal: can all that is (snail-)ploughed be counted as ploughing?

story.act: no story; the proverb is a ploughing image whose sense depends on how நந்துழுத is divided

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the cruel and angry cannot do what those of proper character do

93.reading: There are trees that flower and bear no fruit, people who grow old and still do not understand well, and seeds that do not sprout though sown in a prepared bed, and so for a fool understanding does not appear however much he is told.
93.nuance: The verse stacks three failures of growth, flower without fruit, age without understanding, seed without sprout, so that telling the fool is the fourth sowing that comes to nothing. The human case sits in the middle of the plant images: old age is treated as a season that may pass without yield.

pazhamozhi.literal: though told, understanding does not appear

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the fool as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: instruction cannot produce understanding in a fool

94.reading: The verse says not to speak anything to the stubborn who grasp neither reasoned thought nor the ways of the world, since such a man keeps hold of what he has taken up and will not let it go, as cloth that has drunk indigo will not take another colour.
94.nuance: The image puts the fault in a first impression that has set: the மூர்க்கன் is not empty but already dyed, so new words have nothing to take on.

pazhamozhi.literal: what has drunk indigo does not become anything else

story.act: no story; the proverb is a dyeing image applied to the obstinate as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: it is useless to counsel the obstinate, who hold to what they first took up

95.reading: Once you have plainly seen a man speak evil, the verse says, do not trust him from then on, for such people behave badly whoever they are, as neem is bitter even if the gods eat it.
95.nuance: The proverb places the bitterness in the neem, not the eater: even the highest company does not sweeten it. So the one evil word seen is taken as evidence of a nature, not of a lapse.

pazhamozhi.literal: neem is bitter even if the gods themselves eat it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the evil-speaker as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one seen speaking evil should not be trusted again, whatever his standing

96.reading: Men of the forest life, of cruel deeds, do not behave well even if they are granted a place to live in the settled country, as a quail kept in the hand every day still has its mind on the field.
96.nuance: செய் in the proverb is the field the quail came from: captivity and daily handling do not move its mind. The verse ranks a people by its way of life (காடுறை வாழ்க்கை) and its work (கருவினை), and denies that settlement changes them; whether it means forest peoples as a group or only those of cruel deeds among them, the Tamil does not settle.
96.domain_note: the lord who grants them a place to live in his country

norm.note: a ranking of the period: forest dwellers of cruel work are held unable to be reformed by settlement

pazhamozhi.literal: the quail's mind stays on the field

story.act: no story; the proverb is a captive-bird image applied to the forest men as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: granting settled land does not change those of forest life and cruel deeds

97.reading: The lowest, of black deeds, do not care about the great blame that falls on them, lord of the shore where the great punnai drives off the stink of fish, just as some will eat without fear in a house of weeping.
97.nuance: The proverb's eater at a house of mourning is shameless rather than cruel: he does what the occasion forbids because the opinion of others has no hold on him. The shore frame sets the punnai's scent against the fish smell, a cleansing the base never receive.

pazhamozhi.literal: eating without fear where there is weeping

story.act: no story; the proverb names the shameless act of eating at a house of mourning

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the base are untouched by the blame they incur

98.reading: When men have done a very great wrong and do not know the fitting way to make it good, their trying to stand out is, as the verse tells the lord of the shore where the adumbu flowers on the sand, like throwing water from a small dish at a great blaze.
98.nuance: The sense turns on துடும்பல் and on what தலைசிறத்தல் does here; the reading takes the proverb as a remedy too small for the harm. அகலுள் நீர் may also be the water in a lamp-bowl. Both the image and the counsel are offered tentatively.

pazhamozhi.literal: throwing (at) a துடும்பல் with the water in a small bowl

story.act: no story; the proverb is an image of an inadequate remedy, as far as its rare word allows

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a great wrong is not undone by small or showy amends

99.reading: Those who could not repay their unworthy enemies take delight, as if a victory had come to them, on hearing the words others speak without regard, and though this gives them nothing to eat or drink, theirs is the drunkenness of one who has not even seen the toddy.
99.nuance: The syntax of lines 1-2 is loose; the reading takes the base man's joy to come from others' slander of his enemy, an empty gain he could not win himself. The proverb mocks intoxication without the drink.

pazhamozhi.literal: the elation of one drunk without seeing the toddy

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the base man's borrowed triumph

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the base rejoice in what does them no good and is not their own doing

100.reading: To go on doing evil afterwards as if one wanted to, though one has seen that one was punished with no regard to one's labours, is, lord of the cool sea shore where the broad-faced drum sounds, like a thing that grows a span for every cubit cut from it.
100.nuance: முழம் குறைப்ப சாண் நீளும்: cut a cubit and it grows back a span. Punishment trims the base man's wrongdoing but does not stop its growth. The verse does not name who is punished; the heading makes it the base.

pazhamozhi.literal: as a span grows back when a cubit is cut

story.act: no story; the proverb is an image of regrowth after cutting

pazhamozhi.applied_to: punishment does not cure the base of wrongdoing

101.reading: The unlearned base do wrong if they are harassed, and if they are not, not knowing where to go, they spoil things and rise up, as for the jackal there is no good year or bad year for food.
101.nuance: The reading takes அலப்பின் as 'if pressed' and அலவாக்கால் as 'if not pressed': the base do harm in either case, as the jackal feeds on carrion in famine and plenty alike. The division of lines 1-2 is uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: for the jackal food is no different in a good year or a bad one

story.act: no story; the proverb is a jackal image applied to the base

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the base do wrong whether they are pressed or left alone

102.reading: The verse asks whether there are any fools whose names go unknown among those who refuse the good words from the mouths of the keen-minded and, leaning on their dark understanding, do harsh things, and answers that there is no bull the village does not know.
102.nuance: The proverb's மூரி is the rogue bull that every villager has learnt to step around: the fool's harsh deeds make him notorious, so his folly is public, not private.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no bull the village does not know

story.act: no story; the proverb is a village image of the notorious rogue

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the fool who rejects wise counsel and acts harshly becomes known to all

103.reading: Among all the low who come down in a continuous line, search as one may, those of good character do not appear, lord of the mountain land of groves thick with trees, for among monkeys there is none with a fine face.
103.nuance: நிரந்து வழிவந்த நீசர் is a claim about descent: character is said to run in a line, and a whole line is denied any good member. நீசர் here ranks people by birth; the proverb makes the line a species.

norm.note: a birth-rank claim of the period: those descended from a base line are held to have no one of good character

pazhamozhi.literal: among monkeys none has a handsome face

story.act: no story; the proverb makes the base line a kind, like monkeys

pazhamozhi.applied_to: good character is not found among those of base descent

104.reading: To clear out those who are fit and raise up the base who are of no use is, the verse tells a woman of sweet lisping speech like the yaazh, like cutting down the honeyed jackfruit and planting the bitter kanjirai.
104.nuance: ஊழாயினார் most likely means those who are fit or of the right order; the act described (களைந்திட்டு ... பெருக்குதல்) is one of patronage, removing some and promoting others. The address to a woman is a frame and not the counsel's audience.
104.domain_note: a ruler or master choosing whom to raise

pazhamozhi.literal: cutting down the jackfruit and planting the kanjirai

story.act: no story; the proverb is an orchard image of exchanging a sweet tree for a bitter one

pazhamozhi.applied_to: displacing the fit to promote the base destroys what was useful

105.reading: To take the honour due to the great and give it instead to the small is, lord of the town where spotted bees hum on the flowers, like spreading a seat of honour for a dog.
105.nuance: The fault judged is the giver's: the verse does not say what the dog does with the seat, only that laying it out is absurd and takes from the great what was theirs.

pazhamozhi.literal: like spreading a seat on a dog

story.act: no story; the proverb is an image of misplaced honour

pazhamozhi.applied_to: honour meant for the great is wasted and misplaced on the small

106.reading: Even if one shows them great favour so that their distress is ended, and they prosper greatly without fault, the worthless do not become men of good family with minds made spotless.
106.nuance: The patron's favour is given in full (பெருக்கத் தலையளித்து) and their prosperity is granted as faultless, so the failure lies only in what they are. குடி here is the standing of a good house, which the verse holds cannot be conferred. The closing quotation marks enclose the clause of the main sentence; the proverb may have been marked editorially.

norm.note: a rank claim of the period: the base cannot become of good family through favour or wealth

pazhamozhi.literal: the worthless do not become (a good) family

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the base as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: favour and prosperity do not raise the base into good family

links.note: Kural 458 says that even the worthy, good of mind in full, are protected by good company; Pazhamozhi 90 reverses the same phrase to say the base, good of company in full, never become good of mind.
links.teaches: Held together they show the house view that company acts on the mind has a limit: it guards a good mind already there and cannot make one in the base.
links.list_adds: its salt-sea image and inverted wording set an exception beside the couplet: for the base, company runs one way only and leaves the mind as it was.

links.note: Kural 452 says water changes with the land it runs on, as understanding takes the nature of company; Pazhamozhi 90 uses water the other way, the fresh flood that cannot sweeten the sea.
links.teaches: The same water image proves opposite things depending on which is larger: the Kural's water yields to the soil, while the base man is the sea that absorbs every good influence unchanged.
links.list_adds: it turns the couplet's image around, making the base the vessel that alters what flows in rather than being altered.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 90 denies that good company changes the base; 106 denies that a patron's favour and prosperity change them.
links.teaches: Read in sequence the chapter closes both routes of reform it considers, the influence of good companions and the gift of fortune, so the base man's nature is fixed against both.

links.note: Naladiyar 262 says the wise do not seek the base however rich, as no one picks cactus buds; Pazhamozhi 91 says those who live as kin of the worthy do not go over to the small though they are called superior.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar grounds the refusal in judgement of the base, Pazhamozhi in belonging: settled among the worthy, one does not change sides, and the sweetness on offer is jaggery in sand.
links.list_adds: it gives the refusal a cause the quatrain lacks, the bond of living as kin of the worthy, and admits the small some sweetness while denying it is edible.

links.note: Naladiyar 351 says the petty-minded grow more practised in wrong as they age; Pazhamozhi 93 says some grow old without understanding, like trees that flower without fruit.
links.teaches: Together they deny that age brings wisdom from two sides: the Naladiyar says age deepens folly, Pazhamozhi that it can simply pass without yield, so telling the fool is one more seed that will not sprout.
links.list_adds: it sets old age among the failures of plant growth, flower without fruit and seed without sprout, so the old fool becomes a natural kind of barrenness.

links.note: Kural 849 says the one who shows things to the unseeing becomes unseeing himself while the other keeps what he saw; Pazhamozhi 94 says not to counsel the obstinate, who keep what they took up.
links.teaches: The Kural describes the failed lesson and Pazhamozhi draws the rule from it, adding the cause: the obstinate are already dyed, so the teacher has no blank cloth to work on.
links.list_adds: its indigo proverb explains why the lesson fails, a first colour that has set, and turns the couplet's observation into a counsel not to speak.

links.note: Kural 510 says that both trusting without examining and doubting one already trusted bring endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 95 says that once you have seen a man speak evil you should never trust him again.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi names the case where withdrawing trust is not the fault the Kural warns of: one evil word plainly seen is taken as proof of a nature, as neem stays bitter whoever eats it.
links.list_adds: it adds a specific condition, evil speech plainly seen, that overrides the couplet's warning against doubting the trusted.

links.note: Naladiyar 350 says small bullocks fed cut grass never learn the yoke, and the base, though rich, are known by their deeds; Pazhamozhi 96 says forest men of cruel deeds granted a place in the country do not behave well.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's care is feeding and wealth, Pazhamozhi's is a ruler's grant of settlement; together they show the period's ethics denying reform by provision whether the provider is a herdsman or a lord.
links.list_adds: it moves the claim from private wealth to a ruler's act of settlement and pins it on a people of a named way of life.

links.note: Kural 1075 says fear is the conduct of the base; Pazhamozhi 97 says the base do not care about the great blame that falls on them.
links.teaches: The pair separates two fears: the base may be held in line by fear of punishment, as the Kural says, but blame, which works on others through shame, has no hold on them at all.
links.list_adds: its proverb of eating fearlessly at a house of mourning shows what the base do not fear, the judgement of others, which the couplet leaves out.

links.note: Kural 1078 says the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed; Pazhamozhi 100 says those who have been punished go on doing evil, growing a span for every cubit cut.
links.teaches: Pressure may wring use out of the base, as the Kural says, but Pazhamozhi denies that it changes them: what is cut back grows again.
links.list_adds: its regrowth image separates getting use from the base by force and reforming them by punishment, which the couplet runs together.

links.note: Kural 1078 says the base yield use only when crushed; Pazhamozhi 101, on the reading that அலப்பின் means 'if pressed', says the base do wrong when pressed and also when left alone. The conflict depends on that reading of line 1.
links.teaches: The two disagree on whether pressure works on the base at all: the Kural makes it the one way to get good from them, Pazhamozhi makes it one more occasion for harm, like the jackal that feeds in any year.
links.list_adds: it sets the pressed and the unpressed case side by side and finds harm in both, removing the couplet's one remedy.

links.note: Naladiyar 260 says the base man kicks away the subtle teaching of the learned and sets up a petty assembly with one like himself; Pazhamozhi 102 says those who refuse the good words of the keen-minded and act harshly are known to everyone.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar follows the refuser into a small circle of his own kind; Pazhamozhi follows him into the village's notice, so refusing counsel ends both in a narrowed company and in public notoriety.
links.list_adds: it adds the consequence the quatrain lacks, harsh action that makes the fool as known as a rogue bull.

links.note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; Pazhamozhi 103 says those who come down in a base line have no one of good character among them. The conflict holds on the reading of 972's செய்தொழில் as conduct or work rather than hereditary occupation.
links.teaches: The pair puts the period's two accounts of character side by side: the Kural makes worth follow deeds and denies birth a role, Pazhamozhi makes it follow descent so firmly that a whole line is written off.
links.list_adds: its monkey proverb treats a line of descent as a species, the very ranking by birth that the couplet rejects.

links.note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Pazhamozhi 104 says clearing out the fit to raise up the useless base is like felling the jackfruit to plant the kanjirai.
links.teaches: The Kural warns against the wrong appointment, Pazhamozhi counts its double cost: the base raised and the fit removed, a sweet tree lost and a bitter one planted in its place.
links.list_adds: its orchard proverb pairs the promotion with a removal, so the folly is an exchange of good for bad rather than a single mistaken trust.

links.note: Naladiyar 345 says a dog fed from a golden bowl still eyes leftovers, so honouring the base does not change their deeds; Pazhamozhi 105 says giving the small the honour due to the great is like laying a seat for a dog.
links.teaches: Both use the honoured dog, but the Naladiyar faults the dog, which stays a dog, and Pazhamozhi faults the one who honours it, who has also taken the honour from the great.
links.list_adds: it moves the blame from the honoured base to the giver and adds the loss to the great whose due was given away.

links.note: Naladiyar 347 says the base, though they have come into wealth, are known by their deeds, as a golden sandal is still for the foot; Pazhamozhi 106 says the worthless whom a patron lifts out of distress into faultless prosperity do not become men of good family.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar says wealth does not change deeds; Pazhamozhi adds that it does not change rank either, even when the wealth is a patron's gift and is used without fault.
links.list_adds: it names the patron's favour as the source of the wealth and denies the base the standing of குடி, a claim of rank the quatrain does not make.

source_issues: 92 line 4: நந்துழுத may be divided நம் உழுத or நந்து உழுத; the proverb's sense depends on it.
98 lines 3-4: துடும்பல் is obscure and the proverb's image is uncertain.
99 lines 1-2: the syntax is loose and the sense of the counsel is uncertain.
101 lines 1-2: the word division of அலப்பின் அலவாக்கால் and சிதைத்தெழுப is uncertain.
106 line 4: the quotation marks enclose the main clause (கூதறைகள் ஆகார் குடி) and may be editorial.
